channel.title: Acura recalls — Car Recall Tracker
channel.description: NHTSA vehicle safety recalls explained in plain English.

item.title: Honda, Acura SUVs: rear frame can rust through
item.description: These vehicles were sold in states that salt the roads in winter. The rear subframe, the metal frame that holds the rear suspension to the body, can rust badly where the suspension bolts onto it. If it rusts through, a rear suspension part such as a control arm can come loose. The back of the vehicle can then wander or slide and you could lose control. Honda's full repair is not ready yet and is expected in fall 2026.

item.title: Honda and Acura front passenger airbags may deploy unintentionally
item.description: Honda is recalling certain Honda and Acura vehicles, including the Accord, Civic, CR-V, Odyssey, Pilot, Ridgeline, HR-V, Fit, Insight, Passport and the Acura TLX, RDX and MDX. The sensor that measures the weight of the person in the front passenger seat can crack and short circuit. If that happens, the airbags can go off when they should not during a crash. Dealers will replace the seat weight sensors at no cost. This recall expands an earlier recall.

item.title: Acura ZDX and Honda Prologue rearview camera may blank out
item.description: The backup camera can show a distorted picture or no picture at all when you shift into reverse. That leaves you without a clear view of what is behind the vehicle while backing up, including people or objects low to the ground. Honda has mailed letters warning owners, but replacement cameras are not ready yet; the fix is expected in late 2026. Honda will send a second letter when you can book the free camera replacement.

item.title: Acura ZDX dashboard display and backup camera may fail
item.description: A software bug can make the main dashboard screen go blank, so you may not see your speed or the warning lights that tell you something is wrong with the car. The same problem can also leave the backup camera showing a blank screen when you shift into reverse, so you get no picture of what is behind you. A dealer will reload the radio control module software to fix both problems.

item.title: Honda and Acura models: driver's seat may be loose
item.description: The fasteners holding the driver's seat cushion frame may not have been tightened enough at the factory, so the driver's seat can be loose. A seat that is not solidly attached may not hold the driver in place in a crash, which means a higher chance of injury. The vehicles also do not meet the federal safety rule for seating systems. Dealers will replace the driver's seat cushion frame at no charge.

item.title: Acura ILX brakes can weaken from an internal leak
item.description: Contaminated brake fluid can make a seal inside the part that pushes fluid to your brakes change shape. Once that seal is deformed, fluid leaks inside the part instead of doing its job, and the brakes get weaker. You could need more distance to stop than you expect, especially in an emergency. Honda dealers will replace that part for free. VIN lookup opens December 17, 2025, and owner letters were mailed May 4, 2026.

item.title: Acura RDX may suddenly lose power steering assist
item.description: The computer settings for the RDX's electric power steering may not be set correctly. When that happens, the steering system can switch itself into a protective backup mode and stop helping you turn the wheel. The car still steers, but it takes much more muscle to turn, which can be a dangerous surprise while you are driving. Honda dealers will reload the correct steering software. It is a free reprogramming, and no parts have to be replaced.

item.title: Acura and Honda brake pedal can shift out of position
item.description: The brake pedal in these Acura and Honda models is held in place by a small pin, and that pin was not fastened correctly at the factory. Over time the pedal can slip out of its normal position. If that happens, pressing the pedal may not slow or stop the vehicle the way you expect. Honda also says the affected vehicles do not meet federal rules for brake systems and for lamps and reflectors.

item.title: Acura MDX tailgate moisture can knock out vehicle lights
item.description: Water can get into the light assembly and wiring in the tailgate at the back of the vehicle. Once moisture reaches the wiring, lights can stop working — the lights on the tailgate, the position lights, the license plate lights, the taillights, and lights inside the vehicle. Dealers will check the wiring and, as needed, add a fuse harness, replace the tailgate light, and reseal the body, all at no cost to you.

item.title: Acura ZDX stabilizer bar bolts may come loose
item.description: The bolts holding the bracket for the front stabilizer bar on the passenger side may not have been tightened enough, so they can work loose and pull away from the frame. If the bar or its bracket falls partly off, it can hit and damage the high-voltage cables or the battery coolant lines underneath. That can shut the vehicle down and leave you without power to move. Dealers will inspect and tighten the bolts and repair any damage for free.

item.title: Acura MDX touchscreen may go blank, hiding backup camera
item.description: The large touchscreen in the middle of your 2025 MDX's dashboard can suddenly go blank. When it does, the picture from the backup camera no longer appears when you shift into reverse, so you cannot see what is behind the vehicle on the screen. Federal rules require that rear view image to show every time you back up. Honda has traced it to the display unit and will swap in a new one.

item.title: Acura and Honda Pilot software glitch can stall engine
item.description: The computer that controls how fuel is fed to the engine has a software bug on these Acura and Honda models. Because of it, the engine can stall or suddenly lose power while you are driving. Losing power in traffic or on the highway raises the risk of a crash. The dealer will reload corrected software into that computer at no charge; owner letters were mailed in March 2025.

item.title: Acura ZDX loose suspension bolts can cut power
item.description: Bolts that hold a front suspension bracket to the vehicle's frame can work loose and fall out. If the bracket comes free, it can rub against or damage the thick high-voltage cables or the cooling lines that keep the battery at the right temperature. Damage to either one can shut down the electric drive system, so the vehicle could suddenly stop pulling while you are driving.

item.title: Acura TLX fuel tank weld can leak gasoline
item.description: The pipe you pour gas into connects to the fuel tank, and on these TLX sedans that joint may have been welded badly at the factory. A bad weld can let gasoline leak out. Leaking fuel near anything hot or sparking can start a fire. The dealer will replace the entire fuel tank assembly at no charge to you. Owner notification letters were mailed in early February 2025.

item.title: Honda and Acura Driver's Seat May Be Loose
item.description: On certain Honda Accord, Accord Hybrid, Civic Sedan, Civic Hatchback, Pilot and HR-V vehicles and Acura Integra models, the driver's seat cushion frame may not have been tightened properly when the car was built. That can leave the driver's seat not firmly secured to the floor. These vehicles do not meet the federal safety standard for seating systems. Dealers will replace the driver's seat cushion frame at no cost to the owner.

item.title: Honda and Acura steering gearbox may make steering difficult
item.description: The steering gearbox — the part that turns your steering wheel motion into the wheels turning — may have been built wrong on these Honda and Acura models. Parts inside can rub too hard against each other, which can make the vehicle difficult to steer. Difficulty steering raises the chance of a crash. The dealer will replace a spring inside the gear and add or move grease around as needed, all free of charge.

item.title: Acura ZDX brakes can release pressure without warning
item.description: On some 2024 Acura ZDX All-Wheel Drive models, the anti-lock brake system can switch on when it should not and let go of the pressure in the brakes. If that happens while you are slowing down, you can lose braking power with no warning. The fix is a software update for the brake control computer. It can either arrive over the air to the car itself or be installed by a dealer. Owner letters were mailed September 26, 2024.

item.title: Honda Odyssey and Acura RDX steering can rust, bind
item.description: The steering gearbox on these vehicles may not have been tightened properly when it was put together. A gearbox that is not tight lets water get inside, and the water causes rust. Rusted gears can start to bind, which means the steering may feel stiff or may not respond the way it should while you are driving. Honda dealers will replace the entire electric power steering rack on affected vehicles, free of charge to the owner.

item.title: Honda and Acura passenger seat sensor may crack
item.description: Honda is recalling certain 2020 through 2022 Honda and Acura vehicles, including Accord, Civic, CR-V, HR-V, Odyssey, Pilot, Passport, Ridgeline, Fit, Insight and the Acura MDX, RDX and TLX. The sensor that measures the weight of the person in the front passenger seat can crack and short out. When that happens, the system may not switch off the front passenger airbag when it is supposed to.

item.title: Honda and Acura fuel pump can fail, stalling engine
item.description: The fuel pump sits inside the gas tank and sends fuel to the engine. On these vehicles that pump can fail. When it does, the engine can stall while you are driving — losing power in traffic or on the highway raises the chance of a crash. A dealer will replace the entire fuel pump unit for free. This recall is an expansion of two earlier Honda fuel pump recalls covering additional vehicles.

item.title: Honda and Acura engines can seize from faulty bearing
item.description: A manufacturing mistake means a bearing inside the engine — part of what lets the engine's moving pieces spin smoothly — can wear down and seize up. That damages the engine, which may then run roughly or stall while you are driving. A stalled engine in traffic can lead to a crash, and the damage can also lead to a fire. Dealers will inspect the engine and repair it, or replace it entirely if that is what it needs.

item.title: Honda Civic, Pilot and Acura MDX Brake Failure Risk
item.description: A fastener that connects the brake pedal booster to the brake master cylinder may have been put together wrong at the factory. If it fails, the master cylinder can separate from the booster and you could lose the ability to stop the vehicle. A dealer will inspect the brake booster assembly and repair it if needed at no cost. Honda mailed owner letters on August 7, 2023, so the repair is available now.

item.title: Acura RDX and Integra brake unit can leak fluid
item.description: These cars have a part that helps control braking and stability. A small valve inside it can leak brake fluid. When that happens, the car may creep or roll on its own while the automatic brake hold feature is holding it still, or the brake pedal may sink farther down than normal before the brakes bite. Either one makes a crash or injury more likely. Dealers will replace the whole unit at no cost.

item.title: Honda and Acura front seat belts may not latch
item.description: Because of a manufacturing problem, part of the front seat belt buckle can press against the release button. When that happens, the metal tongue will not click in and stay locked, so the belt may not fasten at all. A seat belt that is not latched cannot hold you in place in a crash. Honda dealers will replace the driver and front passenger buckle release buttons, or the whole buckle, free of charge. Letters were mailed April 18, 2023.

item.title: Acura TLX tires may have cuts from factory handling
item.description: The tires on some 2022 Acura TLX cars may have been cut or torn while they were being sorted at the factory. Damage like that can weaken a tire, and a weakened tire can suddenly lose air. A blowout at speed can pull the car sideways and make it hard to steer. Your dealer will look at the tires and replace any that are damaged at no charge to you.

item.title: Acura RDX and Honda CR-V Hybrid driveshafts may break
item.description: A part inside the left or right front driveshaft — the shaft that sends power from the engine to a front wheel — may not have been heat-treated correctly, so it can break. If it breaks while you are driving, the vehicle can suddenly lose power. A broken driveshaft can also let the vehicle roll away after you park if the parking brake is not set. A dealer will replace the affected front driveshaft at no cost.

item.title: Honda and Acura fuel pump can fail and stall engine
item.description: The pump that pushes gasoline out of the fuel tank toward the engine sits inside the tank, and on these Honda and Acura vehicles it can stop working. When it fails, the engine can stall, meaning it shuts off while you are driving, and that can happen at any speed. Your dealer will replace the whole fuel pump assembly at no cost to you. This recall is a larger version of an earlier Honda recall, 20V-314.

item.title: Honda and Acura fuel pump failure can stall the engine
item.description: The low-pressure fuel pump sits inside the gas tank and pushes fuel toward the engine. On these Honda and Acura vehicles, that pump can quit working. If it does, the engine can stall — shut off — while you are driving, which can leave you stopped in traffic or unable to keep up with the cars around you. Dealers replace the entire fuel pump assembly at no charge, and this repair has been available since July 2020.

item.title: Acura ILX driveshaft can separate and roll away
item.description: Too much grease was used when the driveshaft was assembled. The grease can keep a small locking ring from snapping fully into place, so the driveshaft can pull apart from the half shaft that turns the wheel. If that happens, the car may suddenly stop pulling itself forward. It can also roll away on its own after you shift into Park, because the parking lock no longer holds the wheels through the driveshaft.

item.title: Honda and Acura SUVs: timing belt can lose teeth
item.description: Your vehicle's timing belt is a toothed rubber belt that keeps the engine's internal parts turning in step. On these vehicles, the teeth can break off the belt. If that happens, the engine can shut off while you are driving, and the belt failure can also damage other engine parts. Dealers will check the belt and replace it at no cost, and will also inspect the engine and replace anything that was damaged.

item.title: Acura MDX: water in tailgate lights can knock out taillights
item.description: Water can get inside the lights mounted on the tailgate of these Acura MDX models. The moisture can knock out those tailgate lights and the main taillights along with them. With your taillights out, drivers behind you have a much harder time seeing your vehicle, especially at night or in bad weather, and that raises the chance someone runs into you. The dealer will rework or replace the tailgate lights.

item.title: Acura MDX and TLX fuel pump may stall engine
item.description: Tiny particles in the gasoline can stick to parts inside the fuel pump, the part that pushes fuel from the tank to the engine. Over time the pump can weaken and stop delivering enough fuel, which can make the engine quit while you are driving. Dealers will load updated engine computer software and, if the pump is already weak, put in a new fuel pump at no cost to you.

item.title: Acura ILX fuel gauge may show wrong gas level
item.description: Certain 2014-2019 Acura ILX cars may have a fuel tank that is bent out of shape. That pushes the fuel pump up higher than it should sit and can make the float that measures your gas level stick in place. The result is a fuel gauge that shows more gas in the tank than you actually have. You could run out of gas and stall without expecting it. Dealers will inspect the tank and replace it if needed, free of charge.

item.title: Honda and Acura rear brakes may stop poorly
item.description: The pistons inside the rear brakes were not coated the way they should have been. That can let gas pockets form, and gas squeezes down when you press the brake pedal instead of pushing the brakes firmly against the wheel. The result is weaker braking than the vehicle is supposed to have, so it may take longer than normal to stop. These vehicles do not meet the federal braking standard. The fix is free.

item.title: Honda Pilot, Ridgeline and Acura MDX seats may loosen
item.description: The power front seats in these vehicles were put together with rivets that were not made correctly. Those rivets hold the seat frame to the floor. In a crash, the rivets can break and the seat may come loose instead of staying anchored down. In the Pilot and Ridgeline it is both front seats; in the MDX it is the driver's seat. Honda says the seats and seat belt anchors do not meet federal safety rules.
